primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- CJP's tenth lecture in the Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. Distinguished Lecture Series, delivered at the Far Eastern University, presenting the Action Program for Judicial Reform as the transformation of the Philippine judiciary and as Davide's enduring legacy

His assessment of Chief Justice Davide by the 'four Ins' of an ideal magistrate -- Integrity, Independence, Industry and Intelligence -- and his argument that Davide's greater distinction lies not in his jurisprudence but in his role as chief executive officer of the entire judicial department

A systematic tour of the APJR reorganized from its six technical components into three intelligible headings: the transformation of judges, the improvement of judicial facilities and tools, and the judiciary's relationship with its various publics

His claim that the APJR has earned unmatched local and international acclaim and funding, capped by the International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms of November 28-30, 2005, and his pledge that the program will outlive Davide's retirement on December 20, 2005
sub_topics: His personal opening at FEU, recalling his inaugural address as president of the FEU Central Student Organization in 1957, and his thanks to Dr. Lourdes Reyes-Montinola, Dr. Lydia B. Echauz and Dean Andres D. Bautista for co-sponsoring the lecture

His prediction that Davide will be remembered as one of the greatest Chief Justices in the country and the Asia-Pacific, and his recollection of writing 'Leadership by Example' in 1999 to lay out a paradigm for judging the new Chief's credo

The bases for rating magistrates -- contribution to jurisprudence, depth and breadth of legal philosophy, influence on the country -- and the four Ins he set out in his earlier speech 'Judging the Judges'

The markers of Davide's reputation: presiding over the Estrada impeachment trial from November 2000 to January 2001, his simple and transparent lifestyle, and his punctuality to the point of embarrassing his hosts

The distinction between the Chief Justice as primus inter pares with a single vote and as unquestioned CEO of the judiciary, spending more than 60 percent of his time on the administrative, financial and management concerns of 28,000 judicial employees
The paradox CJP draws: detached and unfathomable as a decision writer, transparent and accountable as a leader -- 'As a jurist, he is an individualist; as an executive, he is a team player'

The 'Davide Watch' announced at a Kilosbayan forum on December 11, 1998, eleven days after his oath, with its vision statement of an independent, effective and efficient judiciary worthy of public trust and a legal profession providing quality, ethical, accessible and cost-effective service

The APJR's origins in the UNDP-funded 'Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary' and an 18-month nationwide consultation under Chief Justice Narvasa, its approval on December 8, 2000, its Executive Committee headed personally by the Chief Justice, and its day-to-day management by the Program Management Office

The six components -- Judicial Systems and Procedures, Institutions Development, Human Resource Management Development, Institutional Integrity Development, Access to Justice by the Poor, and Reform Support Systems -- and his reasons for regrouping them into three lay-intelligible topics

Bar examination reform adopted June 8, 2004: a tenured Board of Bar Examiners, character and fitness screening, multiple-choice questions alongside essays, scaling and eventual computerization, set against the contrasting bar regimes of Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Japan and Korea

The Legal Education Board to be headed by a retired SC justice, the referral of clinical legal education to it, and the piloted Judicial Apprenticeship Program for third- and fourth-year law students in Metro Manila
MCLE as the continuing requirement for practising lawyers, with 1,527 accredited lectures or programs presented in 2004

The Judicial and Bar Council: the constitutional filter of at least three nominees per vacancy, the 90-day appointment rules, its composition, and the April 27, 2004 Resolution giving it decentralized management, a separate budget and a restructured organization

The Philippine Judicial Academy's pre-judicature, orientation, career-enhancement and special-focus programs; its e-learning modules on electronic evidence and psychological incapacity launched December 1, 2004; and its video production on pretrial and discovery

The Mediation Project: Philja designated on October 16, 2001 as the unit for court-annexed mediation, 29 Philippine Mediation Center units and 527 trained mediators, a 77 percent trial-court success rate from 2002 to 2005, and 67 percent of 105 cases compromised in the Court of Appeals pilot

The JURIS Project begun January 2003 teaching judges to mediate after CAM fails, with 73.30 percent success in San Fernando City, Pampanga and 63.72 percent in Bacolod City, plus CIDA-supported study at the Commonwealth Judicial Education Institute in Halifax and ADB-supported environmental and court-administration training

Ethics enforcement: 463 lawyers sanctioned in six years under the Code of Professional Responsibility; the New Code of Judicial Conduct of June 1, 2004 patterned on the Bangalore Principles; the amendment of Rule 140; the 2002 rule converting administrative cases into disciplinary proceedings against bar membership; and 660 justices and judges sanctioned from 1999 to 2004

Incentives and protections: the annual Judicial Excellence Awards taken over by the Court in 2004, the doubling of judicial compensation through 25 percent annual increases from November 2003, better retirement and automatic disability benefits, and the dismissal of complaints filed within six months of a judge's compulsory retirement

The strengthened Committee on Legislative-Executive Relations, now including the presiding justices of the Court of Appeals, Sandiganbayan and Court of Tax Appeals, to press for fiscal autonomy and better pay

Studies and assessments: the UNDP Blueprint, the ADB-funded 'Strengthening the Independence and Defining the Accountability of the Judiciary,' and the 'Institutional Strengthening of the Shari'a Justice System'

Computerization: the USAID-supported Case Flow Management pilot in Pasay City, the CIDA-supported CAMIS in Metro Manila, their integration with legacy stand-alone systems, the Computer Literacy Program for 28,000 personnel, a computer in every courtroom with a second to come, and interest-free P1,000-per-month laptops for justices and judges

The e-library launched November 19, 2004, 'the first of its kind in Asia,' with decisions uploaded within 48 hours, full searchability, no need for space and CDs for courts without Internet; plus the Benchbook for Trial Court Judges, a uniform writing-style manual, computer-aided transcription and an infrastructure master plan

Model electronic courts in Angeles, Lapulapu and Cagayan de Oro funded by a World Bank loan, the planned conversion of the old GSIS building on Arroceros Street into a Hall of Justice, and new rules of procedure on electronic evidence, intellectual property, corporate rehabilitation, intra-corporate controversies and juveniles

Opening the judicial fortress: the Public Information Office established January 1, 1999 'not as a public relations arm, but as an information-based office,' publishing Benchmark, Court News and Court News Flash in simple non-legalese on the Court's website

Chamber-to-Chamber Dialogues with The Asia Foundation answering business-sector criticism of judicial interference in the economy, supported by his own book 'Leveling the Playing Field,' and the USAID- and ABA-Asia-funded Justice-to-Justice and Judge-to-Judge Dialogues

Access to justice: UNDP studies of the DOJ and penal institutions, the IBP jail decongestion project in Manila, Pasay, Quezon City and Pasig, the IEC program training clerks of court and barangay officials, the EU-assisted project for internally displaced persons in Southern Philippines, and the Justice on Wheels mobile court launched December 21, 2004

Stakeholder consultations on memoranda, recognizance, summary procedure and affordability, and the PERLAS project with the Department of Education, The Asia Foundation and Libertas to teach rule-of-law values in elementary and high schools

The international verdict: World Bank chief counsel Anthony Gerald Toft's endorsement of the Philippine program as worthy of emulation, support from UNDP, WB, ADB and TAF and from seven national aid agencies, and CJP's claim that no other country has enjoyed similar global assistance

The November 28-30, 2005 International Conference and Showcase he chairs, expecting around 150 foreign Chief Justices and judicial educators, fully funded by donors; and his closing tribute to the retiring Davide as 'the deft and constant gardener' whose reform seed the rest of the judiciary will continue to tend

stances.claim: Chief Justice Davide will be best remembered not for his decisions but for the wide-ranging judicial reforms he began upon taking his oath on November 30, 1998, which he himself called the centerpiece of his stewardship and the yardstick for his legacy.
stances.rhetorical_move: legacy argument: ranking the executive achievement above the jurisprudential one and quoting the Chief's own standard back as the measure

stances.claim: The Chief Justice is more than primus inter pares: with only one vote in a collegial Court but unquestioned authority over the entire judicial department, it is in leading 28,000 judicial personnel toward independence, integrity, transparency and accountability that he makes the real difference.
stances.rhetorical_move: role distinction supported by the paradox of the detached jurist who is a transparent and accountable executive

stances.claim: The APJR has genuinely transformed the judiciary, bringing cutting-edge technology and best management practices to the third branch, as shown by mediation success rates, the e-library, computerization, disciplinary numbers and the doubling of judicial pay.
stances.rhetorical_move: accumulation of concrete projects and statistics, organized into three lay-intelligible headings rather than bureaucratic components

stances.claim: The Philippine program is a model judicial reform program: the World Bank's chief counsel has endorsed it as worthy of emulation, and no other country has enjoyed similar global assistance for modernizing its judicial system.
stances.rhetorical_move: external validation through an outside expert's endorsement and a catalogue of international donors

stances.claim: The APJR is not the personal vision or project of the Chief Justice but of the entire Supreme Court and judiciary, and will therefore be continued with the same ardor after his retirement.
stances.rhetorical_move: succession reassurance framed as a collective commitment, closing on the gardener metaphor and the dawn of a judicial renaissance

notable_anecdotes: CJP opens by placing himself back on the same stage 48 years earlier: in 1957, as a young sophomore law student, he delivered his inaugural address in the FEU Auditorium as president of the FEU Central Student Organization.

He recalls writing 'Leadership by Example' in 1999, just after Davide's appointment as the 'Centennial' or even 'Millennial' Chief Justice, and dedicating the volume to him in the hope of setting a paradigm by which his influence could later be judged.
He offers the small human detail that Davide is always on time, sometimes embarrassing his hosts by arriving well ahead of them at convocations, fora, dinners and simple meetings.
He notes that the APJR is the only standing committee of the Supreme Court personally and directly headed by the Chief Justice, a fact he uses to show its pivotal importance.

He reports the Court's pride in the Philja mediation numbers -- 29 mediation centers, 527 trained mediators, a 77 percent trial-court success rate, and 70 of 105 cases compromised in a two-month Court of Appeals pilot.
He shares the news that the Court was in the final stages of negotiating a P600 million grant from the Japanese government to build the Philja Training Center in Tagaytay.

He closes with a gardener image for the retiring Chief -- one who sowed the seed of a transformed judiciary through his vision-mission statement and nurtured it through the APJR -- and with the Filipino sign-off 'Maraming salamat po.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Judicial Renaissance' is the tenth lecture of the Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. Distinguished Lecture Series, delivered by Justice Panganiban at the Far Eastern University, where he had given his inaugural address as student council president 48 years earlier. He predicts that Davide will be remembered as one of the greatest Chief Justices in the Asia-Pacific, recalls dedicating his 1999 book 'Leadership by Example' to him, and measures him against the four Ins of an ideal magistrate -- Integrity, Independence, Industry and Intelligence -- before making his central distinction: the Chief Justice has only one vote as primus inter pares, but as chief executive officer of the entire judicial department, spending more than 60 percent of his time on the concerns of 28,000 judicial employees, he is a paradox who is detached as a jurist yet transparent and accountable as a leader. Davide's true legacy, he argues, is the reform program begun on his assumption of office: the Davide Watch announced at a Kilosbayan forum on December 11, 1998, with its vision of a judiciary worthy of public trust, and the Action Program for Judicial Reform approved on December 8, 2000, which grew out of the UNDP-funded Blueprint and an 18-month consultation under Chief Justice Narvasa. Regrouping the APJR's six technical components into three plain headings, CJP inventories the reforms in detail: bar examination and legal education reform, the Legal Education Board, the Judicial Apprenticeship Program, MCLE, a restructured Judicial and Bar Council, Philja's training and e-learning, court-annexed mediation and the JURIS Project with their success rates, the New Code of Judicial Conduct patterned on the Bangalore Principles, the sanctioning of 463 lawyers and 660 magistrates, the Judicial Excellence Awards and a doubling of judicial pay; then computerization through CFM and CAMIS, a computer in every courtroom, installment laptops, the e-library launched in November 2004 as 'the first of its kind in Asia,' the Benchbook, model electronic courts and new rules of procedure; and finally the opening of the judicial fortress through the Public Information Office, Chamber-to-Chamber and Judge-to-Judge Dialogues, jail decongestion, the PERLAS school program and Justice on Wheels. Citing the World Bank's Anthony Gerald Toft and a roster of donors, he calls the program a model, previews the International Conference and Showcase of November 28-30, 2005 that he chairs, and closes by promising that the APJR, the work of the whole judiciary rather than one man, will continue after Davide's retirement.
